title: I made Liftbound, a cozy iPhone elevator game, with Claude Code and it was surprisingly complicated.
selftext:
**Liftbound** is a cozy elevator-dispatch game for iPhone, out now on the App Store. Think *Balatro* and *Mini Metro* had a love child and they were obsessed with elevators. 

You send the cars, riders head to work, the gym or the rooftop club, and the building fills up. It has 20 hand-designed buildings, an Endless mode that keeps generating new towers, a Daily Building, and building codes you can share.

[App Store link](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/liftbound-cozy-elevator-game/id6827381090)

I didn’t type a prompt and get a game back. It took almost two months of milestones, redesigns, story writing, rewriting, killing ideas, prototyping. I wrote the design docs, made every design call, played every build and threw out a lot, and Claude Code implemented against the docs. 

**A deterministic simulation**

All the game logic is a Foundation-only simulation with a seeded RNG, so the same seed and the same inputs always give the same run. That lets me change art, UI or code and still prove gameplay didn’t move.

**2,312 unit tests**

The full suite runs all night, like 6-8 hours for the full test. So it ran before bed every night after a day of work. Smaller test classes ran all day while fine tuning the direction of the game. Heavy runs went one at a time behind a lock file, because parallel suites on one machine gave flaky failures.

**Pinned bot scores**

A greedy bot plays fixed seeds on every story building, and its exact scores are pinned. If a change moves one point, the test fails. The bot had to win within a certain margin for the game to pass. I wanted the game to feel cozy when they player didn't want to be challenged, and challenging when they didn't want to be cozy.  

**Balance passes on 100 seeds**

For each in game nightly upgrade card, the bot played every level 100 times in three ways: always take the card, never take it, or get it free. A card’s worth is the “always” score minus the “never” score. Anything inside ±0.1 stars counts as noise. Some of what it caught that were no expected:

* Co-working floor cost 0.32 stars on the Tower because taking it early pushed out Lounges, the strongest card there. Making it a rare card fixed that.
* Bigger Cars cut scores 16% to 30%, because bigger cars rarely fill and the full-car bonus stops firing. Now there are Keepsakes (think jokers in Balatro) that balance it. 
* The daycare lowered scores because kids take half a seat and cars filled less often. Kids now score double.

**Art**

Art was all made with code, except for the Keepsake vector art designed by ChatGPT in Affinity. 

Final visual pass before launch fin tuned the graphics, added many small details, feathering, depth, lighting, texture. I also added the winter event graphics that will auto appear in the app on December 12th, when the winter event will launch. Even if the player doesn't update their game. 

**What went wrong**

* Long sessions lost context. Handoff docs after every commit (rules, plan, to-do) fixed that.
* AI-generated art wouldn’t stay consistent. I scrapped a 3D pipeline and a set of story cutscenes, and now everything is drawn in code.
* Two sessions sharing one checkout overwrote each other’s work. Now each one gets its own git worktree.

If you’re testing an AI-built game that has random RNG, what’s your testing setup?

comments.author: Lazaros28
comments.body: Question about the music. It fits the game nicely and you even have different sounds based on what is going on. In a claude created game, how do you manage to have nice background music and SFX that fit the game theme?

replies.body:
All music was created in Suno, and I just gave Claude the files and told it when I wanted it to play! I also had it create it's own sound effects which I chose and approved (the multiplier stacking sounds for example) 

For the Club scene in the trailer, that music is added on for comedic effect. In the game, the club audio is minimal and only appears when the elevator you are currently controlling opens its doors on the floor the club is located, and it's very minimal. I wanted to keep the cozy vibes instead of having the club take over the scene.
